modules.title: Read an earnings release through the income statement
modules.subtitle: Bridge sales growth into operating profit and identify mix, price, and volume effects.
modules.objective: Bridge sales growth into operating profit and identify mix, price, and volume effects.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Company news becomes easier to interpret when you can place it in the accounts. More sales may bring more profit, but they may also require additional inventory or leave customers owing more money. Follow the path from revenue to expenses, profit, and cash. Each step gives you a different question to ask of an earnings release.

## Understand the idea

Read an earnings release in layers: headline measures, segment results, accounting statements, reconciliations, and outlook. Build a consistent bridge from revenue to gross profit to operating profit before interpreting EPS. Revenue may rise through price increases, unit sales, acquisitions, or currency translation, each with different persistence and costs.

Do not compare an adjusted metric with an unadjusted expectation. Note exclusions, repeated restructuring, stock compensation, and changes in reporting definitions. Management's preferred metric can be informative when reconciled and consistently used, but it does not replace cash flow or the claims senior to shareholders. Keep recurring operating developments separate from disposal gains and financing effects.

$$
\text{EBIT}=\text{Revenue}\times\text{Gross margin}-\text{Operating expense}
$$

## A worked example

Cedar's quarterly revenue increases from 200 to 220, but gross margin falls from 40% to 35%. Gross profit falls from 80 to 77. Operating expense rises from 50 to 52, taking EBIT from 30 to 25, a 16.67% decline despite 10% sales growth. A $12 property gain could lift reported net profit without improving this operating bridge.

## Put the idea into practice

Create old and new columns using one accounting basis and the same period. Reconcile price, volume, mix, acquisitions, and FX where the release permits it; mark unavailable components instead of forcing them to sum through invented estimates. Compare each segment with its prior trajectory. Ask whether weaker margin reflects a temporary launch, permanent competition, or a mix shift, then attach a measurable follow-up indicator.

new = 220 * 0.35 - 52

Missing information includes segment mix and whether lower gross margin is recurring; the property gain should be shown separately.

modules.title: Cash conversion and hidden working-capital demands
modules.subtitle: Link earnings headlines to receivables, inventory, cash collection, and reinvestment.
modules.objective: Link earnings headlines to receivables, inventory, cash collection, and reinvestment.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Revenue recognition and cash collection can occur in different periods. Growing receivables or inventory may absorb cash even when reported profit rises. Start with earnings and reconcile noncash charges, working-capital changes, and capital spending. Specify the sign convention: an increase in operating working capital uses cash; depreciation is a noncash expense added back in a simplified reconciliation.

A single weak quarter does not prove aggressive accounting. Seasonality, product launches, contract terms, or strategic inventory can explain timing. Conversely, repeated collection delays may contradict management's growth narrative. Compare the change with sales, prior seasonal patterns, receivable aging, and customer concentration. Free cash flow definitions vary; state yours explicitly.

$$
\text{Illustrative cash after capex}=NI+D\&A-\Delta NWC-\text{Capex}
$$

## A worked example

Nusa reports net income of 40 and depreciation of 10. Operating working capital rises by 25 and capex is 20. Under the simplified assumptions, operating cash flow is 25 and cash after capex is 5. Last year the comparable amount was 20. Profit alone misses the financing required to support the new inventory and receivables. These numbers omit other possible cash-flow adjustments and are not a complete statement reconstruction.

## Put the idea into practice

Read the cash-flow statement alongside balance-sheet notes. Break working capital into receivables, inventory, and payables; distinguish cash held by the group from cash available to the parent. Ask what reverses next quarter and what is structural. Model a collection-delay sensitivity instead of automatically adding all working-capital investment back to value. Keep dividends, buybacks, and debt repayments separate from operating cash generation.

print("Cash after capex:", income + depreciation - working_capital - capex)

assignment.solution: The base case leaves 5 after capex. Working-capital investment of 50 would produce -20, potentially requiring cash reserves or external financing. Review aging, inventory turnover, supplier terms, and seasonal history before assuming the cash use will reverse.

modules.title: Guidance, conference calls, and changing KPIs
modules.subtitle: Read management's future claims with ranges, definitions, and observable follow-up tests.
modules.objective: Read management's future claims with ranges, definitions, and observable follow-up tests.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Guidance is conditional management communication, not a contractual promise. Record the metric, period, range, assumptions, and exclusions. Compare with prior guidance and dated market estimates on the same basis. A range midpoint is a convenient summary, not necessarily management's expected value or a probability distribution.

Conference-call answers can clarify mix, pricing, or capacity, but tone is weaker evidence than an attributable numeric commitment. Changes in KPI definitions can break comparability: active users, backlog, recurring revenue, and same-store sales depend on inclusion rules. Look for reconciliation, discontinued measures, changing cohorts, and a widening range. Treat a missing answer as unresolved rather than filling the gap with optimism.

$$
\text{Midpoint revision}=\frac{(L_1+U_1)/2}{(L_0+U_0)/2}-1
$$

## A worked example

Cedar previously guided annual revenue to 900–1,000 and now guides 920–960. Both midpoints are 950 and 940 respectively, a 1.05% decline in the midpoint. The lower bound improves while the upper bound falls. Management calls this 'greater confidence', which may describe a narrower range but does not erase the lower central estimate. A new backlog definition includes cancellable orders absent from the old definition.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a guidance-change table and write a question for each major movement. Separate changes in demand from changes in the reporting metric. Tie management's narrative to a future release: conversion of backlog to recognized sales, churn by cohort, or capacity utilization. Preserve the old definition in your history and do not splice incompatible series into one growth chart.

old_mid = (900 + 1000) / 2
new_mid = (920 + 960) / 2
print("Old midpoint:", old_mid)
print("New midpoint:", new_mid)
print("Midpoint revision:", new_mid / old_mid - 1)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Write three questions for management: one about demand, one about the narrower range, and one about the changed backlog definition. Specify how you will review the next quarter.
assignment.solution: Ask which demand assumptions reduced the upper bound, whether the narrower range reflects visibility or conservatism, and how backlog reconciles under the old definition. Review order conversion and cancellations next quarter. The midpoint falls from 950 to 940; the narrower range is not by itself a stronger earnings forecast.

modules.title: Corporate actions and value per share
modules.subtitle: Connect financing, buybacks, acquisitions, and dilution to the shareholder's actual claim.
modules.objective: Connect financing, buybacks, acquisitions, and dilution to the shareholder's actual claim.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A financing headline changes both resources and claims on those resources. Issuing shares brings cash into the firm and expands the share count. A buyback reduces cash and shares; whether it creates value per remaining share depends on the price paid, financing, alternative uses, and future economics. EPS accretion alone is not proof of value creation.

For acquisitions, separate stand-alone value, payment, financing costs, integration spending, and uncertain synergies. For dividends and buybacks, distinguish authorization from completed cash distributions. A split changes units of ownership rather than the underlying business value. Read the actual terms before comparing per-share metrics, including convertible instruments and employee dilution.

$$
V_{\mathrm{share,new}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{equity,old}}+\mathrm{Net\ proceeds}+\mathrm{Project\ NPV}}{\mathrm{Shares}_{old}+\mathrm{Shares}_{new}}
$$

## A worked example

Nusa has equity value of 500 and 50 shares, or 10 per share. It raises 80 by issuing 10 shares at 8. With no fees or new project value, total equity becomes 580 across 60 shares, or about 9.67 per share. Cash increased while estimated value per old share fell. A new investment could offset that transfer only if its net value is supported, not simply because gross spending is large.

## Put the idea into practice

Use a before-and-after table for cash, debt, equity value, and diluted shares. Model the transaction separately from operating assumptions so the same cash or synergy is not counted twice. For a rights offering, examine the rights terms and participation assumptions rather than transplanting this simple placement example. Evaluate deals under downside integration and financing cases before relying on management's headline accretion figure.

proceeds = 10 * 8
print("Before value per share:", old_value / 50)

modules.title: Inflation releases: levels, rates, and base effects
modules.subtitle: Read inflation data without confusing slower price growth with falling prices.
modules.objective: Read inflation data without confusing slower price growth with falling prices.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Economic releases describe a particular quantity over a particular period. A price level, a monthly change, and an annual inflation rate answer different questions. Before interpreting the headline number, identify its units, comparison period, and revision status. Then consider how that change could reach a company through customers, costs, financing, or currency exposure.

## Understand the idea

A price index measures a level; an inflation rate measures how that level changes over a specified interval. Slower inflation can coexist with rising prices. Read the release's population, basket, period, units, adjustment method, and revision policy before interpreting the headline. Monthly seasonally adjusted changes and annual unadjusted changes should not be treated as interchangeable observations.

For companies, map the release to actual exposures. Wages, energy, rents, and selling prices affect different businesses on different schedules. A broad index does not equal a particular firm's input-cost inflation. A favorable inflation surprise can lower financing pressure while also signaling weaker demand, so the earnings and discount-rate channels may oppose each other.

$$
\pi_{m}=\frac{I_t}{I_{t-1}}-1,\qquad \pi_{y}=\frac{I_t}{I_{t-12}}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional index rises from 120.0 last month to 120.6 today and was 115.0 a year ago. Monthly inflation is 0.5%, while the twelve-month change is about 4.87%. If last year's comparison base had been 118.0 instead, the same current index would produce only 2.20% annual inflation. Nothing about that denominator change means today's price level fell.

## Put the idea into practice

Calculate both rates from consistent index series, label any seasonal adjustment, and compare the surprise with a dated forecast on the same basis. Then identify the company's cost basket, pricing power, and contract-reset lags. Build a two-channel note: input margin effect and demand/financing effect. Do not extrapolate a single month's change into a reliable annual forecast; annualization is a conditional arithmetic exercise.

print("Monthly inflation:", current / 120 - 1)
print("Annual inflation:", current / 115 - 1)
print("Annual rate with higher base:", current / 118 - 1)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: Prices rose 0.5% in the month and 4.87% over twelve months. Lower input-cost pressure could support gross margin, while a demand slowdown could reduce volumes. Nusa's purchasing basket, supplier contracts, and customer price sensitivity are needed; the aggregate index does not provide them.

modules.objective: Connect macro releases to business demand while preserving the information available at the time.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Macroeconomic releases summarize an economy through measurement systems with sampling error, revisions, and different publication lags. GDP growth, payroll changes, unemployment, and business surveys are different objects. A diffusion index is not a direct revenue growth rate. A seasonally adjusted annualized quarterly growth rate is not the quarter's raw percentage change.

Separate the new observation from revisions to earlier periods. A strong headline can coexist with weaker earlier estimates. For company analysis, narrow the aggregate to relevant customers, geographies, and products; a domestic construction supplier may respond differently from a global subscription business. A causal mechanism needs an exposure link and time horizon, not just two lines on the same chart.

$$
g_{\mathrm{quarter}}=(1+g_{\mathrm{annualized}})^{1/4}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional jobs release adds 180 thousand jobs for the latest month, while the prior two months are revised down by 40 and 30 thousand. The sum of those reported changes relative to the previous vintage is 110 thousand, but that arithmetic is not itself an official measure of current monthly growth. A fictional annualized quarterly GDP growth figure of 4% corresponds to about 0.985% growth during the quarter: 1.04 to the one-quarter power minus one.

## Put the idea into practice

Record vintage, units, revision size, and consensus timestamp. Keep first-release data for historical decisions and revised data for a clearly labeled retrospective analysis. Map demand to company orders and revenue recognition lags. Ask whether the release changes the distribution of future demand or merely confirms a trend already reflected in orders. Avoid declaring a recession or recovery from a single noisy indicator.

print("Quarterly growth:", 1.04 ** 0.25 - 1)

assignment.prompt: Create an as-published macro note and a separate revised-history note. Explain why a housing supplier and an export software company could interpret the same release differently.
assignment.solution: The as-published note retains each release and its revisions at their actual availability times. Revised history can improve measurement but cannot be inserted into old decisions. Housing orders may depend on domestic credit and construction, while export software depends on foreign demand, contract renewals, and currency exposure.

modules.title: Interest rates, bond yields, and competing stock channels
modules.subtitle: Trace policy news through discount rates, refinancing, demand, and bank margins.
modules.objective: Trace policy news through discount rates, refinancing, demand, and bank margins.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A policy announcement can affect short rates, longer yields, credit spreads, currencies, and expected activity. Separate the decision from prior expectations and the accompanying guidance. Long-term yields need not move by the same amount as the policy rate. A firm's borrowing cost also reflects maturity, credit risk, contract terms, and whether existing debt is fixed or floating.

For equities, distinguish cash-flow news from discount-rate news. Lower rates can increase the present value of unchanged future cash flows, yet lower expected sales or a wider risk premium can offset that benefit. Banks require both asset and funding repricing analysis: lower rates may reduce borrower stress while also compressing margins. Avoid a universal 'rate cuts mean stocks rise' rule.

$$
PV=\frac{CF_1}{1+r},\qquad \Delta\mathrm{Interest}\approx\mathrm{Repricing\ debt}\times\Delta r
$$

## A worked example

An unchanged cash flow of 110 due in one year has value 100 at a 10% discount rate and about 101.85 at 8%. If the same news reduces the expected cash flow to 100, its value at 8% is only 92.59. For a separate company with 200 of floating-rate debt, a full-year 100-basis-point borrowing-cost increase adds 2 of interest before tax, assuming immediate repricing and unchanged principal.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a four-column rate map: debt maturity and repricing, customer demand, discount rate, and credit conditions. For banks, add deposit pricing and credit losses. Show sensitivities rather than multiplying all debt by the policy change indiscriminately. Record whether your cash flows and rates are nominal or real and use the same currency. Verify the actual statement and rate definition before analyzing any live policy event.

assignment.prompt: Write opposite but internally consistent stock scenarios following a rate cut. Specify which observations would distinguish a relief scenario from a demand-deterioration scenario.
assignment.solution: Relief: financing costs decline while orders and cash flows remain stable, raising estimated value. Deterioration: weaker demand lowers cash flows enough to dominate the rate benefit. Compare orders, credit spreads, refinancing terms, and company guidance. The worksheet's values are 101.85 and 92.59, not forecasts of market prices.

modules.title: Rupiah, currency exposure, and Bank Indonesia news
modules.subtitle: Connect exchange-rate headlines to importers, exporters, debt, and hedges in Indonesia.
modules.objective: Connect exchange-rate headlines to importers, exporters, debt, and hedges in Indonesia.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

When USD/IDR rises, more rupiah are required to buy one dollar. The business effect depends on the net cash exposure, not merely the company's listing location. Identify the currencies of sales, inputs, debt service, and cash balances, then separate transaction cash flows from accounting translation. Natural offsets and financial hedges may reduce exposure, but their amounts, maturities, and costs matter.

Read Bank Indonesia communication in its own policy context rather than copying a Federal Reserve narrative. Distinguish the policy announcement, rupiah movement, domestic credit conditions, and global dollar effects. An exporter can face dollar-denominated costs or weak external demand; an importer can have pricing power or hedges. 'Rupiah weakens' is not a complete company thesis.

$$
\Delta\mathrm{IDR\ cost}=\mathrm{Unhedged\ USD\ payments}\times\Delta(\mathrm{USD/IDR})
$$

## A worked example

Fictional Nusa imports $10 million of goods and earns rupiah revenue. USD/IDR moves from 15,000 to 16,000. With unchanged volume, no pass-through, and no hedge, rupiah cost rises from Rp150 billion to Rp160 billion. Hedging half at 15,000 leaves a simplified blended cost of Rp155 billion, before hedge fees. A fictional exporter with $12 million receipts and $8 million dollar operating payments has a $4 million operating surplus; debt service may reduce that surplus further.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a currency ladder by settlement month. Match hedge notional and maturity to the actual underlying cash flows, and distinguish operating flows from debt principal. Test pass-through and volume responses in rupiah. In the notebook write the connection explicitly: berita kurs → biaya atau pendapatan → arus kas → nilai perusahaan. Use the issuer's disclosures for exposure and the central bank's own release for policy facts.

print("Half-hedged total cost (IDR billion):", usd * (0.5 * 15000 + 0.5 * 16000) / 1_000_000_000)
print("Exporter operating USD surplus (million):", 12 - 8)

assignment.prompt: Build importer and exporter exposure tables. Add $3 million of exporter dollar debt service and explain why gross dollar revenue overstates its natural hedge.
assignment.solution: The unhedged importer pays 10 billion more; the simplified half hedge limits the increase to 5 billion before fees. Exporter operating surplus is 4 million dollars, falling to 1 million after the assumed debt service. Gross receipts of 12 million are not the net currency exposure, and mismatched settlement dates still matter.

modules.title: Commodity shocks: producers, users, and realized margins
modules.subtitle: Map oil, coal, and input-price news through contracts, costs, and operating leverage.
modules.objective: Map oil, coal, and input-price news through contracts, costs, and operating leverage.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

The same event can help one business and hurt another. A rise in an input price may support a producer's sales while increasing a manufacturer's costs. Follow the chain of suppliers, customers, contracts, and timing before describing the effect. This unit develops that chain into a map you can use when comparing companies in an industry.

## Understand the idea

A commodity price is not a company's realized selling price or profit margin. Benchmark movements pass through contracts, product grades, transportation, taxes, hedges, and production costs. A supply disruption and a demand boom can both raise prices but have different consequences for volumes and customers. Identify which mechanism the evidence supports.

Compare producers with users. A coal producer may benefit from higher realized prices while a power-intensive manufacturer faces higher costs. An airline can face fuel pressure at the same time as strong travel demand raises fares. Contract resets, inventory accounting, and hedges create lags. Keep a static sensitivity separate from a complete forecast, and distinguish a temporary shock from a durable change in earning power.

$$
\mathrm{EBIT}=Q(P-C_v)-C_f
$$

## A worked example

A fictional commodity producer sells one million units at $80 with a variable cost of $50 and fixed cost of $20 million. EBIT is $10 million. At $90 with the same volume and costs, EBIT doubles to $20 million. If variable cost also rises to $56, EBIT is only $14 million. Separately, a manufacturer buying two million units pays $20 million more after the same $10 input increase before pass-through or hedges.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a value-chain map from input extraction through processing, distribution, and the final buyer. For each firm, document realized-price formulas, unit costs, spare capacity, and balance-sheet resilience. Stress lower volumes as well as higher prices. Avoid applying a windfall multiple to a peak margin without testing a normalized commodity case and required reinvestment.

assignment.prompt: Write a paired producer/user analysis for a fictional coal-price increase. Show three assumptions that could reverse the apparent winner and loser labels.
assignment.solution: The producer benefits only if realized prices rise faster than costs and volumes hold up. The user can be protected by hedges, regulated or contractual pass-through, or offsetting output-price gains. Falling producer volumes, higher royalties, or expensive expansion can reduce its benefit. The static producer EBIT cases are 10, 20, and 14 million.

modules.title: Supply chains, tariffs, and pass-through
modules.subtitle: Trace a policy or logistics shock through unit economics and customer behavior.
modules.objective: Trace a policy or logistics shock through unit economics and customer behavior.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A supply-chain shock changes more than a purchase price. Lead times, alternative suppliers, certification, inventory, working capital, and customer delivery commitments can all matter. Identify the exact product, jurisdiction, timing, and scope in the original announcement. A proposal, enacted measure, exemption, and implemented charge are distinct states; do not model them as interchangeable.

Pass-through is a behavioral and contractual assumption. A firm may raise prices but lose volume, absorb costs but preserve share, or redesign its supply chain at an upfront cost. A supplier's country of headquarters does not by itself determine the treatment of every shipment. For a live case, verify applicable terms through official material; the worksheet below is a fictional cost shock, not a statement of tariff law.

$$
\mathrm{Contribution}=Q\left(P-C_{\mathrm{import}}(1+\tau)-C_{\mathrm{other}}\right)
$$

## A worked example

Nusa sells 100 units at 100 each. Its per-unit imported cost is 60 and other variable cost is 20, leaving contribution of 2,000. A fictional 10% charge on the imported-cost base raises unit cost by 6. With no response, contribution falls to 1,400. Raising price by 3 while volume falls to 95 gives contribution of (103 - 66 - 20) × 95 = 1,615. Partial pass-through does not restore the original economics.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a cost bridge with the explicitly assumed charge base. Model at least no pass-through, partial pass-through with lost volume, and a supplier-switch scenario with upfront costs. Add inventory and financing needs where lead times increase. Separate the policy's announced effective date from the date the firm's income statement first reflects it. Keep uncertain scope as an open question, not a silently chosen input.

print("No-response contribution:", 100 * (100 - 66 - 20))
print("Partial-pass-through contribution:", 95 * (103 - 66 - 20))

assignment.solution: At price 106 and volume 90, unit contribution returns to 20 but total contribution is 1,800, below 2,000. Volume response matters. Also examine supplier-switch costs, longer inventory cycles, and the actual policy scope before using the toy charge in a real valuation.

modules.title: Regulation, litigation, and event-stage uncertainty
modules.subtitle: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.objective: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Read the status of an event before assigning a cash-flow impact. An allegation is not a judgment; an investigation is not a quantified liability; an announced rule may have implementation conditions. Identify the issuing authority, affected entity, procedural stage, stated effective date, and the source's actual claims. Do not turn legal vocabulary into a probability without a documented basis.

The economic impact can exceed an explicit fine through remediation, restricted operations, lost customers, or capital requirements. It can also be smaller if a remedy is limited or reversible. Keep a decision tree with mutually exclusive outcomes and show ranges when probabilities are uncertain. This is an analysis framework; live legal interpretation requires the current primary documents and appropriate expertise.

$$
E[C]=\sum_s p_s C_s,\qquad \sum_s p_s=1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional licensing dispute has analyst-assigned teaching scenarios: 50% no operating restriction with cost 2, 35% remediation with cost 10, and 15% closure with cost 50, all in millions and discounted to the same date. Expected cost is 12. A separate 8 of remediation spending already included in a chosen scenario must not be deducted again. The 12 is a scenario-weighted input, not a prediction that a court will order that amount.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a status timeline and a matrix of direct payments, operational restrictions, and timing. Label which facts are documented and which estimates belong to the analyst. Stress the probability of the adverse branch and the liquidity available to survive it. A small expected cost can hide an unacceptable tail outcome. Update the scenario tree when the event's stage changes, keeping the previous version for review.

costs = [2, 10, 50]
print("Probability total:", sum(probabilities))
print("Expected cost:", probabilities[0] * costs[0] + probabilities[1] * costs[1] + probabilities[2] * costs[2])

assignment.prompt: Write a litigation-event note that clearly labels facts, scenario assumptions, expected cost, and the worst-case liquidity question. Do not assign guilt or certainty from an allegation.
assignment.solution: The provided probabilities are invented analysis assumptions. They sum to one and imply expected cost 12, while the adverse branch costs 50. Compare that branch with accessible liquidity and continuing cash burn. Record the actual event stage and identify the next source update needed; do not call the expected cost a legal outcome.

modules.title: Build a sector and company transmission map
modules.subtitle: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.objective: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Sector membership is a starting point, not an exposure measurement. Two banks can have different deposit mixes and loan repricing schedules; two retailers can sell necessities or discretionary goods; two software companies can differ in renewals, usage pricing, and customer concentration. Read segment economics and funding structure before generalizing from an industry headline.

Build a causal map with measurable links: news → relevant demand or cost driver → company KPI → revenue or margin → cash flow → valuation. Identify the time lag at every step and a counteracting channel. Correlated share-price moves can result from shared ownership or index flows even when near-term operating exposures differ. Distinguish that market linkage from a business linkage.

$$
\mathrm{Net\ interest\ income}=A y_A-F c_F
$$

## A worked example

A fictional bank has 1,000 of earning assets yielding 8% and 900 of funding costing 4%, for net interest income of 44 before credit losses and operating costs. In a rate-cut scenario, asset yield falls 100 basis points while funding cost falls only 50 basis points; income becomes 70 - 31.5 = 38.5. Lower borrower defaults could offset part of that decline. A retailer could instead benefit through consumer financing, while a software vendor may respond mainly through enterprise budgets and valuation rates.

## Put the idea into practice

For three firms, create an exposure table with one primary metric, one lag, one offset, and one disconfirming observation. Score evidence completeness rather than inventing a universal stock signal. Separate effects on this quarter's earnings from effects on long-run competitive position. Rank research priorities by exposure and uncertainty, then open the relevant filings to refine them.

print("Repriced net interest income:", 1000 * 0.07 - 900 * 0.035)
print("Change:", (1000 * 0.07 - 900 * 0.035) - (1000 * 0.08 - 900 * 0.04))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.prompt: Map a fictional rate cut to a bank, retailer, and software firm. For each, identify a business KPI and an observation that could contradict your initial interpretation.
assignment.solution: Bank: net interest income and credit losses; deposit costs falling faster than modeled would challenge the margin-pressure case. Retailer: financed purchases and comparable volumes; falling employment could overwhelm cheaper credit. Software: renewals and customer budgets; stable renewals could challenge a demand-decline assumption. The bank worksheet shows a 5.5 decline before offsets.

terms.definition: A key performance indicator: a measure used to track an aspect of a business. Check its definition and any changes before comparing the reported number across periods.
Money moving into or out of a business or portfolio over a period. It can differ from accounting profit because recognition and payment happen at different times.

The rights held by the owner of an asset, share, or token. Check what those rights include: an ownership record alone does not establish a right to every payment, asset, or decision in the wider business or system.
One hundredth of a percentage point. For example, 20 basis points equals 0.20 percentage points, written as 0.002 when used as a decimal rate.

realWorld.connection: The same macro shock can affect a supplier, producer, retailer, and customer through different paths.
realWorld.task: Map a fictional imported-food supply chain from dollar-priced inputs to a rupiah-paying household. Annotate currency exposure, working capital, debt repricing, and ability to change selling prices.

modules.title: Update valuation and reverse the market's assumptions
modules.subtitle: Distinguish better business prospects from an attractive price after the announcement.
modules.objective: Distinguish better business prospects from an attractive price after the announcement.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Once you understand a business effect, you still need to connect it to value and price. An improvement may already have been expected, and a price move may include other influences. Keep three questions separate: what changed in the business, what changed in your estimate, and what changed in the market. The lessons show how to examine each with an appropriate comparison.

## Understand the idea

A sound news interpretation changes specific valuation assumptions rather than adding a vague premium for a positive story. Update cash-flow level, growth duration, reinvestment, financing claims, or the required return. Keep cash flows and discount rates matched by currency, inflation basis, and claim: equity cash flows use an equity rate, while operating cash flows require the corresponding firm-wide treatment.

Reverse valuation asks what the current price requires before deciding whether your new estimate differs meaningfully. A price increase can exceed the estimated business improvement; a good company development may leave less margin of safety. A simple perpetuity is useful for sensitivity training but requires stable distributable cash flows and a discount rate greater than growth. It cannot represent every growth stage or financing change.

$$
V=\frac{CF_1}{r-g},\qquad CF_{1,\mathrm{implied}}=P(r-g),\quad r>g
$$

## A worked example

A fictional mature firm is expected to distribute next-year equity cash flow of 6 per share, growing 2% with a 10% required return. The toy value is 75. News raises the cash flow estimate to 6.3, giving 78.75 at unchanged rates. If the stock moves from 70 to 85, the new price requires cash flow of 6.8 under those same assumptions. The business estimate improved 5%, yet the market price now exceeds the analyst's updated value.

## Put the idea into practice

Show the old model, each changed input, and the new value range. Reverse one uncertain assumption at a time rather than claiming a unique implied growth rate when several inputs can vary. Stress the required return and terminal growth together with reinvestment needs. Relate the conclusion back to Security Analysis: a narrative does not replace a conservative value range and the evidence that could invalidate it.
modules.code:
print("Old value:", 6 / (0.10 - 0.02))
print("Updated value:", 6.3 / (0.10 - 0.02))
print("Cash flow implied by 85:", 85 * (0.10 - 0.02))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Write a valuation update for the case and calculate the updated value at an 11% required return. State which assumption is most important to challenge before drawing a conclusion.
assignment.solution: At 10% the new estimate is 78.75; at 11% it is 70. The price of 85 requires 6.8 cash flow at the original rates, above the new 6.3 forecast. Challenge cash-flow durability, reinvestment, and the required return. The comparison supports further research or waiting under these assumptions, not a guaranteed future price decline.

The rate used to translate a future payment into an equivalent value today. The chosen rate must fit the payment's timing and the assumptions about its risk and currency.
An increase in the overall price level over a stated period. A measured inflation rate describes a particular basket of prices; the change in one household's actual spending costs can differ.
The gap between the price paid and a conservative estimate of value. The gap can allow for some error in the estimate, but it cannot guarantee that the investment will avoid a loss.

modules.title: Read the price reaction with an event-study baseline
modules.subtitle: Measure abnormal returns while separating description from causal attribution.
modules.objective: Measure abnormal returns while separating description from causal attribution.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An event return mixes company information with market and industry movements. Start with a defined event timestamp, a predeclared return window, consistent price adjustments, and a benchmark. A market-adjusted return subtracts the benchmark; a market-model residual subtracts a return predicted using parameters estimated before the event. Neither automatically isolates the causal effect of one headline.

Confounding announcements, after-hours trading, thin liquidity, anticipatory moves, and benchmark choice complicate interpretation. Summing daily abnormal returns is a short-window CAR convention, distinct from compounding wealth. A single company's short-window residual is descriptive evidence; statistical claims need an appropriate design, uncertainty estimates, and attention to dependence across events.

$$
AR_t=R_{i,t}-R_{m,t},\qquad CAR=\sum_{t\in W}AR_t
$$

## A worked example

Across three fictional event-window days, Cedar returns 1%, -3%, and 2%, while the chosen market returns 0.5%, -1%, and 0.5%. Simple market-adjusted abnormal returns are 0.5%, -2%, and 1.5%, summing to zero. A sensational -3% middle-day headline misses both the market decline and the rebound. Zero CAR does not prove the event was irrelevant; other news or an unsuitable benchmark may mask its effect.

## Put the idea into practice

Write the event window before inspecting the reaction and record competing announcements. Compare more than one defensible benchmark without choosing the one that supports your thesis. If fitting beta, use only pre-event observations and check stability. Report raw and abnormal returns, adjustment method, and limitations together. Do not assume the release price was an executable fill for someone who only read the news afterward.
modules.code:
stock = [0.01, -0.03, 0.02]
market = [0.005, -0.01, 0.005]
abnormal = [stock[0] - market[0], stock[1] - market[1], stock[2] - market[2]]
print("Abnormal returns:", abnormal)
print("Cumulative abnormal return:", sum(abnormal))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Reconstruct the three-day case and write two competing explanations for zero CAR. Then design a pre-event beta estimate and identify which data must be excluded from its fitting window.
assignment.solution: The daily abnormal returns are 0.005, -0.02, and 0.015, totaling zero. One explanation is offsetting company news; another is market exposure that the simple benchmark does not model. Fit beta on an earlier declared window, excluding event and future data. A causal conclusion requires evidence beyond this arithmetic.

The ability to trade the required quantity within the desired time and price conditions. Displayed prices alone do not establish the cost of trading a larger amount.

modules.title: Liquidity, positioning, and second-order effects
modules.subtitle: Interpret rapid market reactions without mistaking a price mechanism for a business change.
modules.objective: Interpret rapid market reactions without mistaking a price mechanism for a business change.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

News can move prices through order flow before an analyst can update a business model. Wide spreads, limited depth, forced selling, short covering, and index-related trades can amplify a move. These are possible mechanisms to investigate, not explanations to assert from a candle alone. A one-day rally need not mean estimated intrinsic value rose by the same amount.

Second-order effects follow responses: a competitor may gain customers after a rival's disruption, but capacity limits or shared suppliers can reduce that benefit. Ask who must act, over what horizon, and with which constraints. Positioning data, where available, often has lags and incomplete coverage. Keep sourced positioning facts separate from speculation about what 'everyone' owns.

$$
\mathrm{Quoted\ spread}=Ask-Bid,\qquad \mathrm{Midpoint}=\frac{Ask+Bid}{2}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional stock was quoted 100.00/100.10 before news and 98.00/102.00 after it. The midpoint remains 100, while the quoted spread widens from 0.10 to 4.00. A market buy of 100 shares at the offered price would cost 200 more than the midpoint reference, assuming enough shares at that offer and excluding fees. The midpoint alone conceals a large execution cost; a limit price controls a bound but may leave the order unfilled.

## Put the idea into practice

Record bid, ask, timestamp, market status, and available depth when studying execution. Separate a mark-to-market observation from a realizable return. In a second-order company map, identify capacity, contract, and input constraints before assigning a rival's lost sales to a beneficiary. A clear decision can be to wait for reliable prices and source confirmation while preserving the research thesis.

bid = 98
ask = 102
mid = (bid + ask) / 2
print("Midpoint:", mid)
print("Quoted spread:", ask - bid)
print("Buy cost above midpoint:", 100 * (ask - mid))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Explain why the unchanged midpoint does not imply unchanged trading conditions. Add a second-order beneficiary thesis and one operational constraint that could invalidate it.
assignment.solution: The midpoint is 100 but the spread widens to 4, making an offer-priced purchase 2 per share above the midpoint before fees. Actual fills also depend on depth and movement. A rival might gain orders from a disrupted supplier, but limited capacity or the same component shortage could block the gain.

modules.title: Scenarios, Bayesian updates, and correlated evidence
modules.subtitle: Update conviction proportionally while avoiding false precision and duplicate evidence.
modules.objective: Update conviction proportionally while avoiding false precision and duplicate evidence.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A news item should update a prior assessment rather than automatically replacing it. For a binary teaching case, Bayes' rule combines a prior probability with the likelihood of seeing the evidence under each state. The likelihood ratio measures discrimination; it is not the probability that the source is correct. Real investment states and observation processes are usually more complex than this binary model.

Do not multiply evidence weights as though dependent reports were independent. Several articles derived from the same company release can repeat one signal. Subjective probabilities need ranges and sensitivity checks, particularly when the evidence's reliability is uncertain. Confidence should describe what the evidence supports, while position or research decisions also consider costs, downside, liquidity, and model error.

$$
P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)P(H)}{P(E\mid H)P(H)+P(E\mid\neg H)(1-P(H))}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose an analyst assigns a fictional 20% prior probability to a lasting margin recovery. A specific independently verified operational signal has probability 60% if recovery is real and 20% otherwise. The posterior is 0.12 / (0.12 + 0.16), or about 42.86%. The evidence raises the probability but does not establish certainty. Reprinting that same operational report in two newspapers is not a second independent signal.

## Put the idea into practice

Write the prior, event definition, likelihood assumptions, and source independence assessment before calculating. Test weaker signal reliability and alternative base rates. Use scenario-weighted values only when outcomes and their units are compatible, and show downside separately. In a memo, state 'conviction increases under these likelihood assumptions' rather than presenting a subjective posterior as a measured natural constant.

prior = 0.20
true_signal = 0.60
false_signal = 0.20
posterior = prior * true_signal / (prior * true_signal + (1 - prior) * false_signal)
print("Posterior recovery probability:", posterior)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Recalculate the posterior if the false-signal probability rises to 40%. Explain what this changes in the memo and why repeated articles should not restore the original confidence.
assignment.solution: The posterior becomes 0.12 / (0.12 + 0.32) = 27.27%. A less discriminating signal produces a smaller update. Repeated articles with a common source do not add independent likelihood information, so they cannot justify multiplying the update again.

exercise.explanation: The numerator is 0.12 and total signal probability is 0.28, giving 42.86%.

modules.title: Build an evidence-led news research memo
modules.subtitle: Turn reading into a dated, reviewable company interpretation with citations and counterarguments.
modules.objective: Turn reading into a dated, reviewable company interpretation with citations and counterarguments.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A research memo should let someone retrace your reasoning. Begin with the question and the dated sources, then show the calculation, alternatives, and conclusion. In this unit, you will bring the earlier steps together and review where AI can assist. Every important claim should remain connected to evidence that a reader can inspect.

## Understand the idea

A useful news memo lets another person retrace the reasoning without trusting your tone. Start with the question, decision time, and source ledger. Keep the sourced facts separate from the company's interpretation and your own forecast. Connect each modeled change to a specific driver, assumption, and follow-up test. A list of links without a causal explanation is not yet analysis.

Use an original short summary with publisher, title, link, date, and relevant location. Credit the source of figures and distinguish licensed data from your calculations. A reference does not itself grant permission to republish an article, chart, photograph, or dataset. The course's fictional packet is supplied for practice; for live research use material you may access and reuse appropriately, without fabricating quotations or sources.

$$
\mathrm{Evidence\ coverage}=\frac{\mathrm{Claims\ with\ verified\ support}}{\mathrm{Claims\ requiring\ support}}
$$

## A worked example

Your fictional packet contains an issuer release, an older annual report, a central-bank summary, and a derivative commentary article. Six claims appear in the draft memo, but only four have verified source locations. Evidence coverage is 4/6, or 66.67%; that is a workflow measure, not a probability that the investment thesis is right. Two unsupported claims about customer losses must be marked as hypotheses or removed.

## Put the idea into practice

Use the downloadable memo template: question; source timeline; facts; expectation baseline; business bridge; valuation range; alternative explanations; decision; next review. Link the note to the lesson in Quanta's notebook. For every conclusion write what would change your mind. Preserve previous memo versions so you can distinguish information improvements from hindsight rewriting.
modules.formula: \mathrm{Evidence\ coverage}=\frac{\mathrm{Claims\ with\ verified\ support}}{\mathrm{Claims\ requiring\ support}}

assignment.solution: A complete memo identifies source times and locations, distinguishes four supported claims from two unresolved ones, states how demand/cost/financing assumptions affect value, and sets a review trigger. Coverage of 66.67% is a documentation statistic only. A research conclusion can be 'insufficient evidence; monitor the next disclosure'.

modules.title: Use AI and sentiment tools as supervised research aids
modules.subtitle: Evaluate extraction and summaries without outsourcing source verification or investment judgment.
modules.objective: Evaluate extraction and summaries without outsourcing source verification or investment judgment.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An AI summary can omit qualifiers, confuse an issuer with a subsidiary, mix reporting periods, or invent a citation. Use a fixed extraction schema: entity, event, event time, publication time, numeric claim, unit, source location, confidence, and unresolved ambiguity. Require the tool to distinguish an unsupported field from an empty value. Verify consequential claims against the original material.

Sentiment labels describe language under a labeling rule, not cash flow or expected returns. Positive wording can accompany an earnings miss. Evaluate on a labeled sample with duplicates grouped and time-based separation; a random split can leak repeated press releases across training and evaluation. Document false positives, false negatives, class balance, and the human review burden. Do not paste restricted articles into a service without checking permitted use.

$$
\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad\mathrm{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional material-event classifier flags 20 items: 12 are true material events and 8 are false alarms. It misses another 6 true events. Precision is 12/20 = 60%; recall is 12/18 = 66.67%. Those metrics assess the declared labels, not trading profitability. If repeated versions of one release appear in both evaluation and training, even those scores may be overstated.

## Put the idea into practice

Compare tool output with a manually checked source ledger. Create a small failure log containing negation mistakes, wrong units, stale guidance, duplicate stories, and mismatched entities. Use a held-out date interval and deduplicated event groups. Set a human verification gate for source links and business-impact calculations. Connect further model work to the Machine learning for stocks course rather than treating this classifier worksheet as a complete trained model.

Reject unsupported summaries before valuation use. The example classifier's 60% precision and 66.67% recall do not validate either summary or a trading strategy.

modules.title: Review decisions, avoid hindsight, and know when to wait
modules.subtitle: Evaluate the quality of the reasoning separately from the next price move.
modules.objective: Evaluate the quality of the reasoning separately from the next price move.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A good decision can lose money, and a weak process can get lucky. Preserve the prediction, probability, horizon, source set, and invalidation condition before observing the outcome. Review both the accuracy of factual extraction and the appropriateness of the business mechanism. Do not rewrite the original thesis after prices move.

Use a decision log to distinguish 'evidence was wrong', 'mechanism was incomplete', 'timing differed', and 'outcome was within the stated downside distribution'. Probability scores can evaluate calibration over a suitable set of resolved events, but tiny, selected, or dependent samples do not support broad claims. A decision to wait is substantive when it specifies what information or price condition would justify reopening the case.

$$
\mathrm{Brier\ score}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Three fictional binary forecasts assign probabilities 0.8, 0.6, and 0.3 to precisely defined events. Outcomes are 1, 0, and 1. Their mean squared probability error is (0.04 + 0.36 + 0.49)/3 = 0.2967. A constant 0.5 forecast scores 0.25 on these same three cases, which is better for this loss on this sample. The result is not enough to conclude the analyst has no skill across all news events.

## Put the idea into practice

Schedule a review date and outcome-resolution rule at memo creation. Record changes as new versions with new evidence. Compare with a declared baseline, keep unsuccessful and no-action cases, and avoid choosing the scoring window after the fact. Note unresolved events separately. For paper execution, include delay, spreads, fees, and the possibility of no fill; a research signal does not grant access to a past price.
modules.code:
probabilities = [0.8, 0.6, 0.3]
outcomes = [1, 0, 1]
score = ((probabilities[0] - outcomes[0]) ** 2 + (probabilities[1] - outcomes[1]) ** 2 + (probabilities[2] - outcomes[2]) ** 2) / 3
print("Forecast score:", score)
print("Constant-0.5 baseline score:", 0.25)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Write a no-action decision with an evidence trigger and a price trigger. Score the fictional forecasts and explain what conclusions the three-case sample cannot support.
assignment.solution: Example: wait until the issuer reconciles cash conversion and revisit only if the price offers the required conservative margin. Record the next release date and downside indicators. The forecasts score about 0.2967 versus 0.25 for the baseline, but three selected events cannot establish stable skill, calibration, or profitable implementation.

options: Lower mean squared probability error on the evaluated sample

modules.subtitle: Defend a complete evidence-to-cash-flow-to-price interpretation, including an alternative case.

modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Combine the course into one dated investment-research memo. Your deliverable is a reasoning chain with traceable inputs, a range of outcomes, and a revision rule. Separate what changed in the business from what changed in market expectations. A final exam checks concepts; it cannot certify the quality of a written memo or turn a fictional exercise into a live recommendation.

Use the supplied fictional Banyu Industrials packet and the reusable memo template. Each release has an availability time so you can reconstruct two information sets. Show revenue, costs, operating profit, cash conversion, financing claims, and diluted shares before assigning a value. The valuation cases deliberately simplify taxes and stable growth; discuss what a real multi-period model would require.

$$
FCFF=EBIT(1-T)+D\&A-Capex-\Delta NWC,\qquad V_{share}=\frac{FCFF_1/(WACC-g)-NetDebt}{Shares}
$$

## A worked example

Before the news, Banyu has sales of 1,000, variable cost of 600, and fixed operating cost of 200, so EBIT is 200. A confirmed input shock raises variable cost by 30, a conditional contract adds 20 of sales at 40% contribution, and efficiency saves 12. Base-case EBIT becomes 190. At 25% tax, depreciation 30, capex 40, and working-capital investment 20, illustrative next-year FCFF is 112.5. A 10% firm-wide discount rate and 2% perpetual growth imply operating value 1,406.25; subtract net debt of 300 and divide by 100 shares to get 11.0625 per share. At price 12, this base case offers no discount.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a downside case that removes the conditional contract, uses working-capital investment of 35, and raises the discount rate to 11%. EBIT is 182, FCFF is 91.5, and value per share is about 7.1667. Apply a hypothetical 25% required margin to that downside estimate to obtain a research price threshold of 5.375. Do not call this a recommended order: the threshold is conditional on a crude fictional model. Explain debt maturity, reinvestment, growth, and event-probability omissions, then write what evidence would justify a model update.
modules.code:
base_ebit = 1000 - 600 - 200 - 30 + 20 * 0.40 + 12
base_fcff = base_ebit * 0.75 + 30 - 40 - 20
base_value = (base_fcff / (0.10 - 0.02) - 300) / 100
down_ebit = base_ebit - 20 * 0.40
down_fcff = down_ebit * 0.75 + 30 - 40 - 35
down_value = (down_fcff / (0.11 - 0.02) - 300) / 100
print("Base EBIT:", base_ebit)
print("Base FCFF:", base_fcff)
print("Base value per share:", base_value)
print("Downside EBIT:", down_ebit)
print("Downside FCFF:", down_fcff)
print("Downside value per share:", down_value)
print("Conditional 25% margin threshold:", down_value * 0.75)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.prompt: Submit a two-page notebook memo with a source timeline, expectation baseline, business bridge, base/downside valuation, competing price explanations, decision, and next-review conditions. Use the downloadable rubric for self-assessment and label every fictional input.
assignment.solution: The bridge yields base EBIT 190, FCFF 112.5, and value 11.0625; downside EBIT 182, FCFF 91.5, and value about 7.1667. A 25% downside margin gives 5.375 under the toy assumptions. At the supplied price of 12, a documented wait-and-research decision is consistent with this model. The memo must address contract probability, reinvestment needed for growth, financing risk, source timing, and alternative price explanations; automatic exam success does not grade those judgments.

outcomes: Verify sources, timestamps, units, and the difference between facts and claims.

readingGuide:
A headline can describe an important event without telling you what it means for a particular company. This course slows down the reasoning between reading the news and forming an investment view. You will check the source, understand the size and timing of the change, and follow its possible effects on sales, costs, cash flow, and value.

Work through each case in three passes. First write what the source actually establishes. Next calculate the possible business effect using clearly stated assumptions. Finally explain what remains uncertain and what investors may already have expected. Indonesian inflation, interest-rate, and rupiah examples help you practise the same method in a familiar setting. Keep your evidence and your interpretation in separate parts of the research memo.

24 lessons × 30 minutes = 12 hours of guided study across six units. Each session includes 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source reading, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation.

This estimate includes assignments; exam time is additional. There are 48 practice questions, six four-question checkpoints, and a 24-question final.

The capstone memo is self-assessed separately. All company names, releases, estimates, probabilities, and prices in the cases are fictional; the course contains no live news feed or stock recommendations.

exams.title: Unit 1: Read and verify the news
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A confirmed order omits its margin and capital requirements. Your research memo should:
options: Treat its full face value as equity value
State the missing inputs before estimating value
questions.explanation: Order value alone cannot establish incremental cash flow or value per share.

questions.question: A widely shared screenshot has no verifiable issuer link. The strongest next step is:
options: Locate and verify the original disclosure
questions.explanation: Source authentication addresses the factual uncertainty; popularity does not.

questions.question: A news article compares quarterly costs with annual profit. First:
options: Use the share price as denominator
questions.explanation: Comparable period and unit definitions are necessary before interpreting the ratio.

questions.question: A claim that a policy decision was fully priced in needs:
options: Evidence of prior expectations and a stated comparison
The strongest adjective in the headline
questions.explanation: A priced-in claim concerns pre-event expectations; the later chart is not enough.

exams.title: Unit 2: Connect company news to the accounts
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Adjusted EPS beats while accounting EPS misses. A defensible comparison requires:
options: The reconciliation and a definition-matched estimate
questions.explanation: Different exclusions can change the result; compare consistent definitions and inspect adjustments.

questions.question: A seasonal inventory build weakens cash flow. The next useful comparison is:
options: Prior seasonal patterns and subsequent sell-through
questions.explanation: Comparable seasonality and inventory realization help distinguish timing from deterioration.

questions.question: A confident call answer contains no metric, date, or condition. Your memo should:
options: Label it qualitative and request a testable follow-up
Convert it to a precise growth rate
questions.explanation: Qualitative communication can inform questions but does not supply missing numeric assumptions.

questions.question: An acquisition raises EPS solely through cheaper debt financing. This alone proves:
options: Neither value creation nor adequate risk compensation
questions.explanation: EPS accretion does not price leverage risk, payment relative to value, or integration costs.

exams.title: Unit 3: Interpret macroeconomic releases
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A headline CPI decline is used as an exact forecast of a software firm's wage bill. The missing step is:
options: Annualizing the headline without checking its basket
Mapping the index to its actual cost exposure and timing
Treating consumer prices as company input costs
questions.explanation: A broad consumer basket does not identify the company's wage contracts or labor-market exposure.

questions.question: A broad survey improves. Linking it to a specific stock requires:
options: Assuming its revenue grows by the index reading
Matching customers, exposure, and recognition lags
questions.explanation: Aggregate indicators need a company-specific demand mechanism and a relevant horizon.

questions.question: A rate cut accompanies weaker expected demand. The valuation conclusion is:
options: Conditional on both cash flows and discount rates
Determined only by yesterday's closing price
questions.explanation: The cash-flow and discount-rate channels can offset each other and must be modeled separately.

questions.question: An exporter earns dollars but owes more dollars over the same horizon. Rupiah weakness is:
questions.explanation: A net dollar payment obligation can become more expensive in rupiah despite export receipts.

exams.title: Unit 4: Map industries and second-order business effects
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A temporary supply shock raises peak margins. A long-term valuation should:
options: Test normalized prices and reinvestment needs
questions.explanation: Temporary windfalls and durable cash-generating capacity should be modeled separately.

questions.question: Full unit-cost pass-through with lower volume guarantees unchanged total profit:
options: No; fewer units and fixed costs still matter
Yes, as long as the selling price rises
questions.explanation: Restoring margin per unit does not restore lost volume or eliminate fixed-cost pressure.

questions.question: Expected legal cost is small but the closure branch exceeds liquidity. The memo should:
options: Treat expected cost as the maximum loss
questions.explanation: An average does not capture whether the firm can survive an adverse outcome.

questions.question: Two firms in the same sector react differently to a cost shock. First inspect:
options: The average past return of their sector
Input mix, contracts, pricing power, and hedges
questions.explanation: Operating exposures and offsets can differ substantially within the same sector.

exams.title: Unit 5: Link fundamentals to stock-market reactions
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A business improvement raises estimated value 5% while price rises 20%. It follows that:
options: The valuation gap must be reassessed at the new price
questions.explanation: Business quality and price attractiveness are separate judgments; recompute the comparison.

questions.question: Estimating event-study beta using observations after the event creates:
options: A better pre-event information set by definition
A risk of contamination and hindsight
questions.explanation: Post-event data can reflect the event and were not available for a pre-event model.

questions.question: A competitor's factory closes. A rival's potential benefit depends first on:
options: Capacity, substitutability, contracts, and shared bottlenecks
The rival automatically receiving every lost order
questions.explanation: Orders transfer only when buyers can switch and the rival can actually supply them.

questions.question: Unknown signal reliability should be handled by:
options: Reporting a precise probability without assumptions
Counting social-media reposts as independent trials
questions.explanation: Varying the likelihood inputs exposes dependence on uncertain assumptions rather than hiding it.

exams.title: Unit 6: Build and defend a repeatable research process
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A reviewable news conclusion includes:
options: Evidence, assumptions, counterarguments, and a revision trigger
questions.explanation: Another reader needs the reasoning chain and a way to test when it should change.

questions.question: Rewritten copies of one release appear in training and test sets. The main concern is:
options: Information leakage through duplicate event content
questions.explanation: Near-duplicate releases can let evaluation reflect memorization rather than unseen-event performance.

questions.question: A useful decision to wait includes:
options: A review trigger and the evidence needed to reconsider
A promise to buy after any positive headline
questions.explanation: Explicit triggers make no-action research testable and help avoid hindsight rationalization.

questions.question: A capstone earns full conceptual exam marks but omits sources and downside liquidity. Its research memo is:
options: Incomplete and still needs separate review
questions.explanation: The exam cannot replace source traceability, model scrutiny, and a written downside assessment.

exams.title: Financial news to company & stock analysis final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A four-year contract ceiling of 80 meets annual sales of 400. Even delivery implies:
questions.explanation: 80 / 4 / 400 is 5%; valuation and realized delivery remain separate questions.

questions.question: An article revised at 15:00 supports a fact absent at 10:00. A 10:30 backtest must:
options: Use the version actually available or exclude the uncertain item
questions.explanation: Point-in-time evaluation needs the contemporaneous version or an explicit exclusion.

questions.question: Annual sales are 1,000 and EBIT is 40. A recurring annual cost of 8 equals:
questions.explanation: 8 / 1,000 is 0.8%; 8 / 40 is 20%, making the profit denominator consequential.

questions.question: Profit rises from 80 to 100 while the pre-release estimate was 110. Which is correct?
Sales of 300 at a 30% gross margin with operating expense of 70 imply EBIT of:
questions.explanation: Gross profit is 90; deducting operating expense of 70 leaves EBIT of 20.

questions.question: Income 30, depreciation 8, working-capital increase 18, and capex 25 produce:
questions.explanation: The simplified reconciliation is 30 + 8 - 18 - 25 = -5.

questions.question: Guidance changes from 100–140 to 110–120. Its midpoint:
questions.explanation: The new range is narrower and the midpoint is five lower; those are distinct observations.

questions.question: Equity value 240 with 30 shares raises 60 by issuing 10 shares. With no other effects:
questions.explanation: (240 + 60) / (30 + 10) = 7.50, versus 8 before issuance.

questions.question: An index moves from 200 to 202 in a month and was 190 a year earlier. Monthly and annual changes are:
New jobs are 150 thousand and prior months are revised by -20 and -35 thousand. Their arithmetic vintage change is:
questions.explanation: 150 - 20 - 35 is 95; label this arithmetic rather than inventing an official growth metric.

questions.question: Floating debt of 300 reprices upward by 150 basis points for a full year. Extra pretax interest is:
questions.explanation: 300 × 0.015 = 4.5, assuming unchanged principal and immediate repricing.

questions.question: A $6 million payable is half hedged; USD/IDR rises by 500. Ignoring fees, added rupiah cost is:
questions.explanation: Only $3 million is unhedged, so 3 million × 500 = Rp1.5 billion.

questions.question: Two million units sell at 70 with variable cost 45 and fixed cost 30 million. EBIT is:
questions.explanation: 2 × (70 - 45) - 30 = 20 million using millions of units.

questions.question: Price 50, total variable cost 35, and volume 80 produce contribution of:
questions.explanation: Contribution is (50 - 35) × 80 = 1,200, before fixed costs.

questions.question: A 70% scenario costs 5 and a 30% scenario costs 25. Expected cost is:
questions.explanation: 0.7 × 5 + 0.3 × 25 = 11, with a separate 25-cost downside branch.

questions.question: Assets of 500 yield 6% and funding of 400 costs 3%. Net interest income is:
questions.explanation: 500 × 6% - 400 × 3% = 18 before credit losses and operating expenses.

questions.question: Price 120, required return 9%, and growth 3% imply next-year cash flow of:
questions.explanation: 120 × (0.09 - 0.03) = 7.2 under the specified model.

questions.question: A stock returns -4% while its benchmark returns -1.5%. Simple abnormal return is:
questions.explanation: Subtract the benchmark: -4% - (-1.5%) = -2.5%.

questions.question: A 49/51 quote and 200-share market buy at 51 imply cost above the midpoint of:
questions.explanation: The midpoint is 50; one extra unit per share across 200 shares costs 200 before fees.

questions.question: Prior 50%, signal likelihood 80% under success and 20% otherwise gives posterior:
Eight memo claims need support; five are verified. A sound memo should:
options: Treat every claim as equally established
Mark the three unresolved claims and their required evidence
questions.explanation: Traceability requires separating verified statements from assumptions and unknowns.

questions.question: A system finds 18 true events, flags 6 false events, and misses 12 true events. Precision and recall are:
questions.explanation: Precision is 18/24 = 75%; recall is 18/30 = 60%.

questions.question: Probabilities 0.9 and 0.4 have outcomes 1 and 0. Their Brier score is:
A new case has FCFF 80, WACC 10%, growth 2%, net debt 200, and 100 shares. Value per share is:
questions.explanation: Operating value is 80/0.08 = 1,000; subtract 200 and divide by 100 to get 8.
